summary: An experimental document that describes a simplified model of abstract objects, their attributes and operations for the Internet Printing Protocol, independent of encoding and transport. It also covers security, internationalization and directory issues. It was replaced by RFC 2911.

plainLanguage.summary: This describes what printers and print jobs are, and what you can ask them to do, without worrying about how the messages travel.

questions: internet printing protocol objects and attributes
what is the internet printing protocol
what is a printer object in ipp
subtitle: The abstract objects, attributes and operations behind Internet printing, defined apart from how the messages are encoded or carried.

tldr.problem: Printing over a network was a patchwork of local systems, with no common way to ask a printer what it can do, submit a job, check on it or cancel it.
tldr.mechanism: IPP/1.0 reduces printing to two abstract objects, a Printer and a Job, with ten request/response operations and a large set of typed attributes. How these are encoded and carried is left to a companion document, RFC 2565.
tldr.outcome: This is an Experimental specification that the IESG expected to be revised before becoming a Proposed Standard. It has been obsoleted by RFC 2911.

today: RFC 2566 is an Experimental specification that has been obsoleted by RFC 2911. Its IESG note said the standards-track version was expected to differ, including strong authentication and privacy features. Its companion encoding and transport document is RFC 2565.

sections.title: A Simplified Printing Model
sections.content:
The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application-level protocol for distributed printing using Internet tools and technologies. Version 1.0 focuses only on end-user functionality. Operator and administrator requirements are out of scope. This RFC is one document in a set: design goals are in RFC 2567, the rationale in RFC 2568, the encoding and transport in RFC 2565, and a mapping to the older LPD protocol in RFC 2569. The model and semantics, which this RFC defines, are independent of encoding and transport.

The model deliberately hides the many parts of a real print system (spooler, print driver, queue, output device). It exposes only two object types, Printer and Job, each with operations and attributes. The RFC says IPP is heavily influenced by the Document Printing Application (DPA) standard.

A client talks to the IPP server part of a Printer object. Behind it, the Printer object may be built into an output device, may be hosted on a server that talks to a device, or may fan out to several devices. IPP's notification service is out of scope for this version, so clients learn about progress by polling with the Get-Printer-Attributes, Get-Jobs and Get-Job-Attributes operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Printing has lots of hidden machinery. IPP pretends there are only two things, a printer and a print job, and describes how you talk to each of them.

sections.title: Printer and Job Objects and Their Identity
sections.content:
A Printer object stands for a real or virtual output device together with the spooling and scheduling around it. The RFC notes it could just as well represent a fax device, an imager or a CD writer. A Job object models one print job and contains documents. A Printer contains zero or more Jobs, and a Job belongs to exactly one Printer. A document is either a stream of document data in a format the Printer supports (typically a page description language) or a reference to one. In IPP/1.0 a document is not an object itself, so it has no identifier or attributes, and all processing instructions are Job attributes that apply equally to every document in the Job.

Every attribute is labeled REQUIRED or OPTIONAL. An object that supports an attribute must support at least one of its possible values.

Both object types are identified by a URI. A Printer has a printer-uri-supported attribute with at least one URI, plus a companion uri-security-supported attribute of the same size that says which security mechanism, such as none or ssl3, goes with each URI. When a Printer creates a Job it assigns both a job-uri and a job-id. The Job ID is a 32-bit positive integer that is only unique within the Printer that created it, which lets clients with local constraints refer to jobs by number. The Job also records a job-printer-uri pointing back at its Printer. The secure or open nature of the Job URI follows the URI the client used to submit the job. Printer and Job names are friendly strings and need not be unique.
sections.plainLanguage: The printer is like a front desk and each print job is a folder it opens for you. Both get an address, and the folder also gets a number you can use as a short nickname.

sections.title: The Operations
sections.content:
An operation is a request followed by a response; IPP operations are synchronous. Every request carries a version-number, an operation-id and a request-id, and every response carries a version-number, a status-code and the same request-id. The client picks the request ID as an integer from 1 to 2^31 - 1, and the Printer copies it back so the client can match replies to requests.

The Printer operations are Print-Job, Print-URI, Validate-Job, Create-Job, Get-Printer-Attributes and Get-Jobs. The Job operations are Send-Document, Send-URI, Cancel-Job and Get-Job-Attributes. Six are REQUIRED: Print-Job, Validate-Job, Get-Printer-Attributes, Get-Jobs, Cancel-Job and Get-Job-Attributes. The rest are OPTIONAL, so a client should first read the Printer's operations-supported attribute before using one. An operation the Printer does not support gets the server-error-operation-not-supported status code.

Each request groups its data. Operation attributes affect how the operation runs, and most do not outlive it. Job Template attributes describe how to process the job. The response may carry a group of unsupported attributes and a group of job or printer attributes. Two operation attributes always lead the group, in this order: attributes-charset first, then attributes-natural-language. The target comes next: either printer-uri, or job-uri, or printer-uri followed by job-id. Target URIs must be absolute rather than relative.

A request that is rejected or partly unsupported is answered with a status code. Appendix B groups codes into classes by prefix (successful, client-error, server-error and so on). A client must understand the class of an unrecognized code and treat it like the first code of that class.
sections.plainLanguage: Every question to the printer gets an answer, and each question has a number so you can tell which answer belongs to which. Some questions every printer must understand, and others are extras.

sections.title: Submitting and Managing Jobs
sections.content:
A create request makes a new Job. There are three kinds. Print-Job sends one document inside the request (the client pushes the data). Print-URI sends only a URI and the Printer pulls the data. Create-Job starts a multi-document job with no data, and is followed by any number of Send-Document or Send-URI operations. The final one sets the last-document attribute to true. If a client only learns afterward that the previous document was the last, it may send a Send-Document with no data and last-document set to true. A Create-Job followed by one Send-Document is equivalent to a Print-Job, but the client should use Print-Job for single-document jobs.

At submission the Printer checks the attributes against its xxx-supported attributes and the syntax and scheme of any URI. It need not validate the document data or fetch the referenced URI, because those checks must be repeated at processing time anyway. Errors found later are reported through the Job's state attributes rather than a status code.

Because send operations can be spread over a long time, a Printer that supports multi-document jobs publishes multiple-operation-time-out. If the client goes quiet, the Printer must recover, for example by aborting the job, treating the last document as final, or holding the job as pending-held with the reason submission-interrupted.

Validate-Job checks that an identical Print-Job would be accepted without creating a Job. Get-Jobs lists jobs, filtered by which-jobs (completed or not-completed), my-jobs and a limit. Cancel-Job is rejected with client-error-not-possible if the job is already completed, aborted or canceled. Once a cancel succeeds, the job is guaranteed to end up canceled.
sections.plainLanguage: You can hand over one page stack and say print it, or start a folder and add stacks one by one, saying this is the last one when you finish. You can also test whether the printer would accept it, or take it back later.

sections.title: Attributes and Their Syntaxes
sections.content:
Objects are described entirely by attributes, each with a keyword name and an attribute syntax. Basic syntaxes include text, name, keyword (lowercase US-ASCII, 1 to 255 characters, starting with a letter), enum (1 to 2^31 - 1), uri, uriScheme, charset, naturalLanguage, mimeMediaType, boolean, integer, rangeOfInteger, dateTime and resolution, plus 1setOf for multi-valued attributes. A text value may be up to 1023 octets. In a response an attribute can have an out-of-band value: unknown, unsupported or no-value.

The Printer and Job attributes fall into groups. Job Template attributes are the processing instructions a client may supply, such as copies, sides, number-up, media, finishings, page-ranges, orientation-requested, print-quality, printer-resolution, job-priority, job-hold-until, job-sheets and multiple-document-handling. For most of them the Printer has a xxx-default attribute and a xxx-supported attribute, so a client can discover what is allowed. Job Description attributes report on a job, such as job-state, job-name, job-originating-user-name and counters like job-k-octets. Printer Description attributes report on the printer, such as printer-name, printer-location, printer-state, document-format-supported, printer-is-accepting-jobs and queued-job-count.

The job-priority value runs from 1 (lowest) to 100 (highest), and the Printer maps a requested value onto the number of levels it supports. If a client supplies an attribute the Printer cannot honor, the Printer returns it in the Unsupported Attributes group: with the value unsupported for an unknown attribute, or with the offending values for a supported attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything about a printer or a job is written on a form with labeled boxes, like paper size, number of copies or whether the printer is busy. The printer also publishes which boxes it understands and what it fills in by default.

sections.title: Job and Printer States
sections.content:
The REQUIRED job-state attribute has these standard values: pending (3), pending-held (4), processing (5), processing-stopped (6), canceled (7), aborted (8) and completed (9). A new job starts as pending or pending-held. A job normally moves left to right through processing to one of three terminal states, completed, canceled or aborted. A job reaches a terminal state only after all activity, including stacking output media, has finished. An implementation need support only the states that suit its output device, and should answer unknown rather than guess.

The optional job-state-reasons attribute adds detail, for example job-hold-until-specified when a future print time keeps a job held, or processing-to-stop-point while a cancel or abort is under way. The Printer has its own printer-state: idle (3), processing (4) or stopped (5). A job arriving at a stopped Printer goes to pending and starts only after a human fixes the problem. State is refreshed when a query arrives, since asynchronous notification is not part of IPP/1.0.
sections.plainLanguage: A print job is like a package in the mail. It waits in line, gets worked on, maybe gets stuck, and finally ends up delivered, cancelled or lost.

sections.title: Fidelity and Embedded Instructions
sections.content:
A client's settings can conflict with what the Printer supports or with instructions embedded in the document. The ipp-attribute-fidelity boolean decides what happens in the first case. If it is true, the job must be printed exactly as specified or be rejected. If it is false or omitted, the Printer must accept the job, ignoring unsupported attributes and substituting supported values for unsupported ones. The RFC's example is substituting iso-a4 media when na-letter was requested. Every Printer must support both modes.

For the second case the SHOULD rule is that an IPP attribute takes precedence over a conflicting instruction embedded in the document data. Because document interpreters do not always allow that, the Printer publishes pdl-override-supported as attempted or not-attempted. Even attempted is no guarantee.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask for a paper the printer does not have, you can say do exactly this or give up, or just do your best. And if the document itself says something different, the printer tries to listen to your request first.

sections.title: Character Sets and Languages
sections.content:
Text and name attributes are for people, so IPP lets each request say which charset and natural language it uses. All clients and IPP objects must support utf-8 and may support other charsets registered with IANA. If a Printer does not support the requested charset, it rejects the request with client-error-charset-not-supported and answers in utf-8. A Printer that supports several charsets must convert between them, and some information may be lost.

Language is handled differently. The Printer must accept any natural language, supported or not, and must remember the language of values the client supplied. Values in a different language from the operation are tagged individually using the Natural Language Override (textWithLanguage and nameWithLanguage). In the RFC's example, an English request carries a job name in French as the pair fr and Rapport Mensuel. For messages the Printer itself generates, it uses the client's language if supported and otherwise its own configured language.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone can write in a common alphabet the printer always knows, and if one word is in another language, you put a little language sticker on just that word.

sections.title: Extending the Model
sections.content:
IPP/1.0 can be extended with new keyword and enum values, attributes, attribute syntaxes, operations, attribute groups and status codes. Extensions registered with IANA are OPTIONAL for conformance. Keywords and enums come in three types. Type1 values can only be added by revising the specification. Type2 values can be added by proposing them to IANA, which forwards the proposal to the IPP Designated Expert for review. Type3 values are added the same way but with no additional technical review required.

Private extensions use a distinguishing prefix on keywords, such as a company's domain name, and the reserved integer range 2^30 to 2^31 - 1 for enums. Operation IDs from 0x4000 to 0x8FFF are reserved for private extensions. The version number changes whenever the model or the encoding changes. A major version change signals structural changes older implementations cannot parse, and a minor one signals additions that can be ignored if not understood. The encodings of operation-id, version-number, status-code and request-id may never change, so that all future versions stay backward compatible for those fields.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a rule book for adding new options, with a strict path for official ones, an easier path for casual ones, and a private corner for a company's own secret additions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IPP objects may be deployed over SSL3 (which the RFC notes is not an IETF standards track specification), without it, or both. Security parameters such as keys are outside the IPP protocol itself. A Printer without SSL3 can use other transport mechanisms, for example HTTP Digest Access Authentication. The RFC says it is hard to predict risks. A private corporate network may skip encryption, while a public network may call for it. It notes that denial-of-service attacks against printing resources are not well understood.

Each operation identifies the requesting user in two ways: the requesting-user-name attribute, which a client should always supply from a login name rather than free user input, and the transport's authentication. The Printer stores a human-readable name and a separate name for authorization, and must treat repeated requests along the same path as the same user. Authorization policy, such as only the job owner may cancel, is left to the site. A Printer may also return fewer attributes than requested, with the same status as for a full answer, so the client cannot tell whether an attribute exists.

The IPP profile for SSL3 lists six cipher suites that a conforming object must implement if it supports SSL3. Two of them use 40-bit export-grade ciphers, which the RFC says are vulnerable to attack, so a client using one must not tell the user the connection is completely secure. The IESG note at the top of the RFC adds that a standards-track version was expected to include strong authentication and privacy features and an ipp: URL type, and it encouraged experimenting with TLS ([RFC 2246]).
sections.plainLanguage: A printer might be in a safe office or out in the open, so IPP lets owners choose how much locking up to do. It also keeps track of whose job is whose so strangers cannot cancel your print.
